name: Bank a fire and carry an ember
summary: Smother the coals so they smoulder till morning, or wrap one in bark and walk with it — so you only ever have to win ignition once.
time: 10 minutes to bank; an ember carries 2-12 hours

materials.item: bark tube or metal tin for carrying

steps.text: BANKING, at bedtime: burn down to a deep bed of coals, rake them into a compact pile, and lay one or two dense hardwood logs across it.
Cover the pile with a layer of its own ash, then a little soil — enough to choke the air down to a trickle, not enough to smother it dead.
steps.why: Fire needs air. You are not putting it out, you are throttling it: starve it to a slow smoulder so it consumes fuel over eight hours instead of one.

steps.text: In the morning rake the ash off, find the orange, feed it fine tinder and blow. A well-banked fire relights in a minute.
CARRYING: take one good coal and nest it in punk wood, dry rot, or true tinder fungus inside a bark tube or a tin, with a plug of moss at each end.
Leave a small air gap. Sealed tight it dies; wide open it burns through. Check it every half hour and blow gently if it has faded.
steps.why: The whole trick is metering oxygen — enough to keep the coal alive, too little for it to consume its bed.

steps.text: TINDER FUNGUS and CHAGA are the traditional ember beds because they smoulder for hours without flaming — see the remedy records for identification.

verify: A banked fire: warm ash in the morning with orange underneath when you rake it. Cold grey all the way down means you buried it too deep.
A carried ember: a wisp of smoke from the tube, and warmth through the bark. No smoke and it is gone.
limits: Banking needs a real bed of COALS. A fire of thin sticks makes ash, not coals, and it will not survive the night whatever you cover it with.
A carried ember is unreliable in wind and rain and dies if you seal it or drop it. Treat it as a bonus over your ignition kit, never a replacement for it.
cautions: A banked fire is a live fire. Never bank one inside a shelter, on peat, or over roots and duff — it can travel underground for hours and surface somewhere else.
Carrying an ember in a container puts a hot smouldering object against your body or in your pack. Suspend it outside the pack.
Carbon monoxide is odourless. A smouldering ember in an enclosed space — a tent, a snow shelter, a closed vehicle — can kill you in your sleep.
